blocks.text: A graduate engineer spends 15 minutes showing a steering committee 31 slides on the vibration behaviour of a gearbox. The committee leaves not knowing whether to spend 40 000 GBP on a new bearing arrangement. A good presentation answers one question the audience actually needs answered, and everything on the slides serves that answer.

blocks.markdown: A technical presentation is a **decision tool**, not a data dump. Start from the **question** your audience must be able to answer when you finish, for example 'Should we replace the chain drive with a belt drive?' Then work out the **answer** you will recommend and the **evidence** that supports it. The audience hears the answer early and spends the rest of the time judging whether the evidence supports it.

blocks.title: Answer-first structure
blocks.text: A structure that states the question and the recommended answer within the first minute, then gives the two or three strongest reasons, then the evidence for each, and ends by restating the answer and the action required.

rows: State the question and your recommendation
Two or three reasons, each one slide
Data, figures, method summary supporting each reason
What could change the answer; the decision required
blocks.caption: A short, answer-first structure for a 10-minute technical presentation (indicative split).

blocks.markdown: Slide design follows from this. Give each slide **one message** stated as a full-sentence title (an *action title*, such as 'Belt drive cuts maintenance cost by 60%'), not a topic label ('Maintenance'). Show the evidence as a clear figure with labelled axes and units; avoid dense text. As a planning rule of thumb, allow about one to two minutes per content slide, and leave time for questions.

blocks.title: Building a presentation for a time slot
blocks.prompt: A 20-minute slot includes 5 minutes for questions. You plan 1 minute for the question and answer, and 1 minute for next steps. Allow 2.5 minutes per evidence slide. How many evidence slides can you use?

steps.text: Speaking time: 20 minus 5 minutes for questions gives 15 minutes.
Time for opening and closing: 1 + 1 = 2 minutes, leaving evidence time.

blocks.answer: Five evidence slides (12.5 minutes), leaving 0.5 minutes of spare time.

blocks.markdown: The second skill is **translation**. A decision maker, such as a finance director or operations manager, usually cares about cost, risk, time, safety and compliance, not about stresses, Reynolds numbers or tolerances. Translate each technical result into one of these. Lead with the decision and impact, keep one number that matters, explain unfamiliar terms by analogy, and keep detailed technical support in a backup appendix.

headers: Translation for a non-technical decision maker
rows: The bearing has a rated life L10 of 8 000 h and operates at 9 000 h per year
The bearing will probably need replacing within a year; plan for that outage
The part works close to its limit, so a small overload could cause permanent damage
Efficiency has fallen by 4 percentage points
The plant uses more energy for the same output; this costs about the same as a new full-time employee
blocks.caption: Technical results rewritten for a decision maker.

blocks.title: Translating a technical result into money
blocks.prompt: An engineer finds that 12 m of uninsulated steam pipe loses 450 W per metre. The boiler is 80% efficient, gas costs 0.06 GBP per kWh, and the plant runs 6000 hours per year. Insulation would cost 3600 GBP. Express the result for a finance director.

steps.text: Gas needed to supply that heat:

blocks.answer: For the finance director: 'Insulating this pipe costs 3600 GBP and saves about 2400 GBP a year, so it pays for itself in about a year and a half.'

blocks.title: Questions are part of the presentation
blocks.text: Challenging questions test whether the evidence supports the claim. Listen to the whole question, restate it if needed, answer directly, and point to the evidence: the data slide, the test result, the standard or the calculation. If you do not know, say so and offer to find out; never invent an answer.

blocks.title: Answering a challenge with evidence
blocks.prompt: You claim that a revised damper reduces vibration by about 5%. A manager asks, 'Why should we trust a number from three tests?' Three runs gave reductions of 4.8, 5.1 and 5.0 percent. Respond with evidence.

steps.text: Acknowledge: three runs is a small sample, so the claim should include its uncertainty.
State the response: the runs agree closely, but more runs would tighten the estimate; propose a further six runs before the final decision.

blocks.answer: 'The three runs gave 4.97% with a standard deviation of 0.15%, so they are consistent, but I recommend six more runs to confirm before we commit.'

blocks.title: Common failures
blocks.text: Starting with background rather than the answer; slides with several messages; unlabelled graphs; jargon aimed at a non-technical audience; and defending a claim by authority instead of evidence.

points: A good presentation answers one clear question, stating the recommendation early and organising the rest as reasons and evidence.
For decision makers, translate technical results into cost, risk, time, safety or compliance and keep the detail in a backup appendix.
Answer challenging questions by restating them and pointing to the evidence; admit uncertainty and offer follow-up rather than bluff.

questions.stem: Which slide title is best for a presentation answering the question 'Should we change the lubricant on the conveyor?'

options.text: Synthetic lubricant reduces bearing temperature by 12 degrees Celsius and extends service intervals

questions.correctOptionText: Synthetic lubricant reduces bearing temperature by 12 degrees Celsius and extends service intervals

distractorRationale.a: A topic label does not state the message.
distractorRationale.b: A topic label again; the audience must work out the message.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: a full-sentence action title states the finding that supports the answer.
distractorRationale.d: A generic heading carries no message.

questions.explanation: A strong slide title states its message as a sentence, so the audience knows why the slide is there. Topic labels leave the audience to infer the point.

questions.stem: A presenter begins a 10-minute talk to a design review panel with 4 minutes of background on the history of gear design before stating the recommendation. What is the main weakness?

options.text: The recommendation is not given early, so the audience cannot judge the evidence against the answer

questions.correctOptionText: The recommendation is not given early, so the audience cannot judge the evidence against the answer

distractorRationale.a: The issue is order, not evidence.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: answer-first structure gives the audience the claim against which to judge the evidence.
distractorRationale.c: Length is not the stated problem.

questions.explanation: An answer-first structure states the recommendation within the first minute. Four minutes of background delays the point and leaves less time for the evidence that matters.

questions.stem: A 30-minute meeting slot includes 6 minutes reserved for questions. You allow 3 minutes per content slide and no other time. How many content slides can you use?
questions.explanation: Speaking time is 30 - 6 = 24 minutes. At 3 minutes per slide this allows 24/3 = 8 slides. Always budget from the speaking time left after questions, not from the whole slot.

questions.stem: An engineer must tell the operations director that a hydraulic press's seal is likely to fail within six months. Which version is best adapted to a non-technical decision maker?

options.text: The seal's Shore hardness has degraded and extrusion gap clearance exceeds the specification
The seal is likely to leak within six months, stopping the press for about two days; replacing it during the August shutdown avoids lost production
There are some concerns about the seal, which are being studied
See slide 14 for the metallurgical analysis

questions.correctOptionText: The seal is likely to leak within six months, stopping the press for about two days; replacing it during the August shutdown avoids lost production

distractorRationale.a: Jargon without impact, which does not help a decision.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: it states the finding, consequence and recommended action in terms of time and production.
distractorRationale.c: Vague and gives nothing to decide on.
distractorRationale.d: Defers to technical detail instead of translating it.

questions.explanation: A decision maker needs the consequence and the recommended action. Technical detail can be kept in a backup appendix for those who want it.

questions.stem: A chiller averages 400 kW of electrical power for 6000 hours per year. Bearing wear is expected to raise its energy consumption by 3%. Electricity costs 0.12 GBP per kWh. What extra annual cost should you quote to the finance director? Give the answer in GBP per year.
questions.explanation: The extra power is 0.03 x 400 = 12 kW. Over 6000 h this is 72 000 kWh. At 0.12 GBP/kWh the cost is 72 000 x 0.12 = 8640 GBP per year, a figure a finance director can compare with the cost of a bearing replacement.

questions.stem: During questions, a manager asks about a corrosion rate that you did not measure. What is the best response?

options.text: Give a confident estimate from memory
Say that you have not measured it, explain what is known from the data you do have, and offer to find out and report back
Tell the manager the question is irrelevant
Ignore the question and move on

questions.correctOptionText: Say that you have not measured it, explain what is known from the data you do have, and offer to find out and report back

distractorRationale.b: Correct: honesty about the limit of the evidence, with a plan to follow up, keeps trust.

questions.explanation: Credibility rests on evidence. Admitting what is not known, while offering what is known and a follow-up, is better than bluffing.

questions.stem: If a senior manager challenges a result, the best response is to remind them of your qualifications and experience rather than to refer to the data.
questions.explanation: Challenges should be met with evidence: data, test method and uncertainty. Appeals to seniority are not evidence and weaken the case.

questions.stem: You must give a 10-minute presentation to engineering colleagues on the question 'Should we replace the chain drive on the packaging line with a toothed belt drive?' Outline the structure, the evidence you would include, and how you would design the slides.
markingGuide: States the question and answer (recommendation) in the opening
Gives two or three key reasons (for example maintenance, noise, cost or efficiency)
Evidence slides with labelled graphs or tables with units and uncertainty
Action titles stating the message of each slide
Covers risks, assumptions and next steps
Time budget appropriate for 10 minutes and a limited number of slides
questions.explanation: The marker looks for an answer-first structure with evidence mapped to reasons. Slide design points such as action titles and one message per slide earn the remaining marks.

questions.stem: A stress analysis reports: 'Peak von Mises stress at the weld toe is 310 MPa, giving a predicted fatigue life of 2 x 10^5 cycles against a required 10^6 cycles.' Rewrite the finding for an operations director who has no engineering background, including the recommendation and one number that matters.
markingGuide: States the consequence: the part will likely crack well before its required life
Quantifies in terms that matter (for example it would last about one fifth of the required life)
Gives a recommendation and its cost or time implication
Uses an analogy or plain explanation, such as bending a paper clip repeatedly
questions.explanation: A good rewrite moves from stress and cycles to consequence and action. The ratio of predicted to required life (one fifth) is the single number a decision maker can use.

questions.stem: At the end of a presentation on a new heat exchanger design, a colleague says, 'Your 18% improvement comes from a simulation. Why should we believe it matches a real exchanger?' Describe how you would respond using evidence, and what you would do if the evidence is limited.
markingGuide: Refers to supporting evidence such as validation against test data, mesh convergence or benchmark cases
States the uncertainty or the range of validity of the simulation
Admits limitations if validation is incomplete
Proposes a follow-up such as a prototype test
Stays professional and does not claim more than the evidence supports
questions.explanation: The marker credits answers that tie the response to specific evidence and honestly bound the claim. Defensiveness or claims beyond the data lose marks.
